title: Hailey:
title_q: “You're in It for the Money, and I'm Not”
title_short: Hailey · Not In It for the Money
headline: A caller says she is only in it for the money. She is not. She was at her own bottom once.
story: A warm line caller keeps telling Hailey she is only in it for the money. She is not. She thought her life would be spent “sad in the dark hole” she created, until MHA showed her she was built for better things.
Now she gets to see people go from their bottom to where they want to be. “That's why I do it.” It must feel warm and sure, a little bit defiant, and hopeful.
do: Open on frame 1 with the warm line caller line. Hook text on frame 1.
Use the warm line phone for 2 seconds only. Phone, no person.
Stay on her face for her own story.
Cut “we don't care” (02:16) out of the “It wasn't until I came to MHA” line.
Hold 1 second after “that's why I do it”.
dont: No “try an online therapist” (02:31). MHA is peer support, not therapy.
No “put your hand out” line (02:38). Barbara and Jen already have the reach-out story.
No WRAP answers (03:31–05:31). They belong to the WRAP video.
Do not show the other peer's face from the warm line clip as if she were Hailey.

transcript:
Auto-transcript of 20260909_C4585.MP4 (Hailey, MHA office, Lincoln, 9 Sep 2026). Times are mm:ss in the source file. Speaker labels removed: many are wrong. The transcript writes "Haley", "HANU", "KEA" and "rap"; the right words are Honu, Keya and WRAP. Her name spelling is not confirmed.
[00:00] (Interviewer) All right, well we are good whenever we're ready. So if you want to start by introducing yourself to the camera, your name and position at MHA.
[00:10] Yeah, I'm Haley, obviously I work at MHA, I work at HANU, sometimes I work at KEA, but mostly HANU.
[00:17] (Interviewer) And how did you first come across MHA?
[00:20] So I was introduced to MHA, I want to say it was 2020, by another employee and it has been basically a home ever since.
[00:33] They're welcoming, they are kind.
[00:36] It's a great organization and I split with MHA once before, but I found my way back and I plan on sticking around because it's the best place I've ever worked.
[00:49] (Interviewer) What makes peer support different from traditional support?
[00:53] I think peer support is important because it's about connecting with other people instead of just supporting other people.
[01:01] We really go the extra mile in making sure that we understand where you're at, not just what you're going through.
[01:09] We want to support you as a whole instead of maybe just an incident that happened.
[01:16] (Interviewer) Is there any moments from MHA that you still think about, funny stories, things that have stuck with you?
[01:25] I used to do the rap groups in the jail and those are never boring.
[01:31] You meet some really awesome characters and every day at MHA is memorable, I think.
[01:38] (Interviewer) What would you say to someone that doesn't believe that they can recover?
[01:43] Honestly, you know, there was a long time where I didn't believe I could recover.
[01:54] I didn't know what recovery looked like.
[01:58] I thought my life was meant to be spent sad in the dark hole that I created.
[02:06] It wasn't until I came to MHA that I really was able to be shown that it doesn't matter what you go through, it doesn't matter what happens to you, we don't care.
[02:19] We know that as a human you're built for better things and we want to help you reach that potential.
[02:26] And so I'd say MHA, man, give MHA a try.
[02:31] I mean, and if you don't want to try MHA, try an online therapist, you know? Something. Anything.
[02:38] Just put your hand out and someone will grab it.
[02:41] (Interviewer) What do you think people get wrong about this work?
[02:45] That we're in it for the money.
[02:47] I have a warm line caller and he's always like, you're in it for the money and I'm not.
[02:55] I love the people I work with.
[02:57] I love the people I get to support, you know, learning people's stories and where they came from and where they're going, you know, is so important.
[03:07] I love to see people who I met when they were at their bottom, you know, I get to see them go to where they wanted to be and that's why I do it.
[03:19] (Interviewer) If someone watching has never heard of MHA, what is one thing that they should know?
[03:27] They're inclusive of everybody.
[03:31] (Interviewer) How has rap impacted your life?
[03:37] When I was introduced to rap, I didn't, you know, like Amber was saying earlier, I didn't know what I looked like on a good day.
[03:45] Rap taught me to kind of look at things in a different perspective.
[03:51] I'm able to see, you know, what I look like when I'm doing good.
[03:56] Or, you know, it was only when I was bad, you know, I could easily identify those things and now it's, you know, I'm confident that I'm good at these things.
[04:08] You know, these are parts of my life that I can look at and know instead of just looking past and yeah, does that make sense?
[04:20] (Interviewer) Next question, if you were selling rap to an organization ... how would you sell rap to them? How does it benefit MHA, basically?
[04:41] You know what, I think rap teaches everyone that we don't look the same, you know, and just because you might be having, okay, say we're all having great days. They all look different, you know?
[04:58] And it doesn't matter if you showed up to work and didn't brush your teeth or you showed up to work and you brushed your teeth and did your hair, you know? We both showed up to work, we're both putting the work in and that's what's important.
[05:12] Rap kind of makes things reachable and that's what I love about it. It's not some crazy set plan that someone gives you, you know? It's attainable, it's set by you and it's made for you and that's why I think you should use it.
[05:31] (Crew talk after the interview, 05:31–05:54.)
